query_text: Write the history of a colour.

content.text:
## A Brief History of **Blue**

Blue is one of the most beloved colours today, but for much of human history it was rare, difficult to make, and strangely absent from early language and art.

In the ancient world, blue pigments were hard to obtain. Unlike reds, browns, blacks, and yellows—which could be made from earth, charcoal, or minerals—strong blues required uncommon materials or complex chemistry. One of the earliest artificial pigments was **Egyptian blue**, developed in ancient Egypt more than 4,000 years ago. Made by heating sand, copper compounds, and lime, it was used in tomb paintings, statues, jewellery, and ceramics. To Egyptians, blue was associated with the Nile, the sky, fertility, protection, and the divine.

Another famous blue came from **lapis lazuli**, a deep blue stone mined mainly in what is now Afghanistan. In the ancient and medieval worlds, it travelled along long trade routes and became extraordinarily valuable. When ground into pigment, it produced **ultramarine**, a name meaning “beyond the sea.” In medieval Europe, ultramarine was often more expensive than gold and was reserved for the most sacred parts of paintings—especially the robes of the Virgin Mary. Its rarity helped make blue a colour of holiness, purity, and heavenly beauty.

During the Middle Ages, blue’s social meaning changed dramatically. Earlier, in parts of Europe, blue had not been a particularly prestigious colour. But by the 12th and 13th centuries, it became increasingly associated with royalty, nobility, and Christian devotion. Kings of France adopted blue in heraldry, and stained-glass windows filled churches with glowing blue light. The colour began to signify authority, loyalty, and spiritual elevation.

Blue became more democratic with the development and spread of cheaper dyes. **Woad**, a plant-based dye used in Europe, and **indigo**, imported from Asia and later cultivated in colonial plantations, made blue textiles more widely available. Indigo in particular transformed global trade. It became a major colonial commodity, tied to forced labour and exploitation in parts of the Americas, the Caribbean, and India. The history of blue cloth is therefore also a history of empire, commerce, and coercion.

In the 18th century, a major breakthrough arrived with **Prussian blue**, one of the first modern synthetic pigments. Discovered accidentally in Berlin around 1704, it was cheaper and more reliable than ultramarine. Artists quickly embraced it, and it appeared in European painting, printing, wallpaper, and later in Japanese woodblock prints. Its intensity and affordability helped expand the visual world of the 18th and 19th centuries.

The 19th century brought another revolution: synthetic chemistry. Artificial ultramarine was developed, and synthetic indigo eventually replaced much natural indigo cultivation. Blue was no longer rare. It became industrial, reproducible, and common.

Perhaps the most famous modern blue object is **denim**. Dyed with indigo, denim workwear became associated with labour, durability, rebellion, youth culture, and eventually everyday fashion. Blue jeans turned a once-precious colour into a global uniform.

In politics and culture, blue has taken on many meanings. It can represent conservatism in some countries and liberalism or the Democratic Party in the United States. It is used in police uniforms, corporate logos, national flags, hospital interiors, and digital interfaces. It suggests trust, calm, order, sadness, distance, and infinity.

Today, blue is everywhere: on screens, in branding, in clothing, in art, and in the language of emotion. Its journey runs from sacred stone and royal glass to synthetic dye and mass-produced denim. Once rare and expensive, blue has become one of the most ordinary colours in daily life—yet it still carries traces of the sky, the sea, the divine, and the distant.
